item.title: Northern California MLS Expands Brokerages’ War Over Exclusive Listing Rules
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
MLSListings joins six other multiple listing services suing Compass over alleged pressure to drop fines for pre-marketing rule violations.

The post Northern California MLS Expands Brokerages’ War Over Exclusive Listing Rules appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
MLSListings, a Northern California multiple listing service, filed an amended complaint on Oct. 30 joining six other MLSs in a lawsuit against Compass in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. The original suit, filed Oct. 21 by Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service, BridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS, Hive MLS, and REcolorado, accuses Compass of pressuring the organizations to stop fining agents who violate pre-marketing and listing submission rules. MLSListings said it received a demand letter from Compass on Sept. 8.

MLSListings President and CEO Dave Wetzel said publicly marketed homes withheld from the shared marketplace harm buyers, sellers, and smaller brokerages. Compass countered that seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, already permit agents to publicly market office exclusives without fines. The brokerage said none of the problems the plaintiffs warn about have materialized in those markets.

Compass said it plans to file a motion to dismiss in the case. The dispute reflects growing tension over how MLSs enforce data-sharing rules that have historically formed the foundation of brokerage cooperation. Separately, three Compass-affiliated agents plan to request a judge quash subpoenas issued in the National Association of Realtors’ legal battle with ThePLS.com.

item.title: What Designers Are Finally Getting Right About Office Noise
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Noise consistently ranks among the top complaints in open workplaces, and designers are moving past white noise toward natural soundscapes and tools that let clients hear a space before construction.

The post What Designers Are Finally Getting Right About Office Noise appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The experience-driven office has been the dominant design idea of the past several years. Owners competing for tenants and companies competing for attendance have invested in better light, better air, better food, better furniture, and better views. The logic holds that people will choose to come in if the building gives them something home cannot.

Acoustics has been the slowest of those elements to get attention despite consistently ranking as the thing people complain about most. Oxford Economics research found noise distraction to be the top complaint among open plan workers, and more than half of non-executive employees report that ambient noise reduces their satisfaction and productivity. A building can get everything else right and still leave people unable to concentrate.

Designing for sound is complicated by the fact that people want different things from it, and the same person wants different things depending on the task. Rather than designing to an average, Ben Sachwald, AKRF’s Senior Vice President and Director of Acoustics, Noise, and Vibration, argues for building range into the floor plate. “It is better to cluster your noisier spaces together and then provide a gradient as you go further away,” he said. “This gives people options. The approach that we take is to remember that no two brains are identical and different tasks and moods can call for different situations.”

How designers treat the sound within those zones has also changed. The standard tool for decades was sound masking, usually filtered white or pink noise played through ceiling speakers to raise the background level enough that nearby conversation becomes unintelligible. It reduces speech distraction effectively and most people dislike how it feels.

Natural sound has emerged as the alternative, and Sachwald sees it as part of a broader misunderstanding about what biophilic design involves. “Some people still think biophilic design just means more plants in the space,” he said. “That is an element but it is much bigger than that.”

Biophilic soundscaping is the term for the practice, and the research behind it goes back further than the current interest. A 2015 study in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America found that natural sound masking in open-plan offices outperformed silence, with cognitive functioning holding higher across the workday. More recent research conducted in a London workplace by Kinda Studios with researchers from Goldsmiths, University of London found participants scoring 12 percent higher on creative thinking under a natural soundscape than under typical office sound, completing cognitive tasks faster without losing accuracy.

Which sound belongs in which space depends on what the space is for, and the choice is more deliberate than picking something pleasant. “In some areas you do want masking so you can use something more like a babbling brook,” Sachwald said. “To bring in energy, you might want waves crashing or birds chirping or have soft, peaceful music playing.” Water sounds are steady and predictable, which is why they cover speech well in focus areas. Birdsong and wave patterns vary enough to pull attention, which makes them better suited to a lobby than a quiet floor.

Architectural renderings have given clients a way to see a space before it exists, and sound has had no equivalent. AKRF built one, a facility in Midtown Manhattan called PinDrop that functions as a floating room within a room, acoustically isolated with an extremely low baseline sound level and a neutral response. The room runs a 10.1 channel Genelec playback system and carries five different acoustical treatments across its walls and ceiling. A client sits in it and hears an auralization, a calibrated rendering of what their conference room will sound like, what the open floor will sound like at capacity, what a particular ceiling treatment changes about either. The project has been covered by the New York Times, the Associated Press, and Fast Company, and won an ACEC New York Engineering Excellence Gold Award.

Being able to demonstrate acoustic outcomes has pulled sound earlier into the design conversation and kept it there through construction, which is where many acoustic decisions quietly get reversed. Value engineering substitutions happen late, often without anyone evaluating the acoustic consequence. Sachwald says being able to let clients hear the difference changes those conversations. “Maybe the contractors are proposing a different product, now we can get the clients to come in and hear how that would change the acoustics,” he said.

That shift is already changing how office designers works with clients, bringing acoustic questions into early planning rather than leaving them to be solved after someone complains. Sachwald expects more of the design process to run through the room as owners get used to evaluating sound the way they evaluate everything else about a space.

The post What Designers Are Finally Getting Right About Office Noise appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Affordable Housing Transfers Face Long, Costly Repairs Before Tenants See Relief
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A Bronx building transferred to affordable housing ownership still holds 700 violations 18 months later, showing the long road from foreclosure to repair.

The post Affordable Housing Transfers Face Long, Costly Repairs Before Tenants See Relief appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
New York foreclosed on 2201-05 Davidson Avenue in the Bronx in 2025, wiping out $27 million in back taxes and transferring the 47-unit building to nonprofit Neighborhood Restore. The property will eventually move to affordable developer Lemle & Wolff, which also manages it. Tenants hoped for immediate relief, but 18 months later the building still carries more than 700 housing-code violations — more than 15 per unit. Emergency repairs have stopped leaks and restored the elevator, but floors remain unlevel and scaffolding covers the exterior.

Lemle & Wolff plans a gut rehabilitation down to the floor joists, requiring tenants to move in stages while preserving their current rents. The developer is still securing a private construction loan to supplement city financing. Rent collections have fallen since the transfer; some tenants who stopped paying under the previous owner have not resumed. Organizers from Our Bronx are pushing residents to pay rent, especially those interested in forming a housing cooperative. Affordable housing operators citywide report collections down several percentage points since the pandemic, while insurance and utility costs have climbed sharply.

City Council member Pierina Ana Sanchez is leading an effort to revive the Third Party Transfer program, which foreclosed on more than 500 properties and 7,000 units between 2008 and 2019. The program was shut down after a class action lawsuit alleged the city took buildings without paying just compensation; the city proposed a $60 million settlement this fall. Sanchez’s SAFER Homes Act would add safeguards for owners before foreclosure. Another Bronx building transferred through the program, 1968 Marmion Avenue, took eight years to complete its renovation, offering a timeline for what Davidson tenants may face.

New York Wants to Turn Distressed Buildings Into Affordable Housing. What Happens While They’re Waiting?

item.title: Houston Developer Hines Joins Race for European Individual Investor Capital
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Hines launches European Long-Term Investment Fund targeting wealthy individuals across Europe, Asia Pacific, and Latin America with open-ended real estate vehicle.

The post Houston Developer Hines Joins Race for European Individual Investor Capital appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Hines received regulatory approval to launch the Hines Global Real Estate Opportunities strategy, an open-ended evergreen vehicle structured as a European Long-Term Investment Fund. The fund will initially target individual investors in Europe, with plans to expand distribution to Asia Pacific, Latin America and Canada. Hines already operates the Hines Global Income Trust in the US, which held $7.3 billion in gross asset value as of September. The Houston-based firm manages $91 billion in assets globally.

The Eltif structure allows periodic redemptions and requires no minimum investment, though managers typically ask for at least €10,000. More than 250 private market funds launched under the Eltif framework since 2024, following regulatory reforms that made the vehicles more accessible to retail investors. Infrastructure currently dominates Eltif assets, while real estate accounts for just 6.6% of the total €18.2 billion in open-end Eltif holdings as of September. The Hines fund will maintain an externally managed liquidity reserve to meet quarterly redemption requests.

Hines joins Blackstone, Apollo and other alternative asset managers expanding their retail distribution channels in Europe. The firm hired Paul Ferraro from Carlyle in 2024 to lead its global private-wealth solutions strategy, then brought on former Schroders executive Eugenio Cicconetti to build out its European wealth division. Fund launches continued at a similar pace in 2026 despite concerns about private capital managers’ exposure to software companies and loan quality, with some firms shifting focus to infrastructure or multi-strategy vehicles.

item.title: The Opposition of New Power Lines Could Spread Beyond Data Centers
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Aging grids need massive infrastructure upgrades

The post The Opposition of New Power Lines Could Spread Beyond Data Centers appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
1 day 2 hr agoNov. 2, 2026 2:47 pm

Spending on the transmission system by investor-owned utilities and transmission companies is expected to reach $43.7 billion this year, up about 10 percent from last year’s estimate, according to the Edison Electric Institute. Much of the country’s power infrastructure dates to the decades after World War II and is due for replacement regardless of what the AI buildout does, but the growth in demand has turned a maintenance cycle into a generational expansion. The fights over where those lines go are now showing up in places that have nothing to do with data centers.

Virginia’s Loudoun County tracked 233 data center buildings completed or under construction as of March, and the grid serving them has to be rebuilt to match. Dominion Energy’s annual electricity demand growth across Virginia and North Carolina has jumped to roughly 5.5 percent from the 1 to 2 percent range it sat in before 2022. Greg Mathe, Dominion’s director of electric transmission engagement, permitting and land, attributes most of that to data centers while noting that electrification and manufacturing growth, including pharmaceuticals, are contributing as well.

In Ashburn, a 500-kilovolt line the utility classifies as a backbone reliability project is routed through a residential backyard that abuts a wooded conservation easement, requiring a 165-foot monopole and the removal of hundreds of trees. The homeowners association donated land at the rear of the neighborhood to the local school system in an attempt to block the path, since Virginia utilities generally lack standard eminent domain authority over county governments and school boards. The state utility commission approved the route anyway, and the dispute is headed to the Virginia Supreme Court on appeal.

Similar disputes are running in Texas, where high-voltage lines proposed to crisscross the state would bisect ranch land northwest of Austin, and in Georgia, where Southern’s Georgia Power plans to tear down 29 homes along a 35-mile line. Clay Rikard, senior vice president of system planning at Southern, points to a voluntary agreement rate above 99 percent and says condemnation is rare, framing the work as broadly beneficial. “Data centers do represent a lot of the growth, but I think they’re also bringing tremendous benefits to our communities,” he said, adding that new transmission also allows older plants to retire and makes it possible to move power in from other regions.

Utilities have an institutional reason not to tie a given line to a given customer. Alexandra Klass, an energy law professor at the University of Michigan Law School, notes that transmission projects are usually justified on congestion grounds rather than by naming a project, since the congestion is real and the need is broad. That framing is accurate and also politically necessary, and it is exactly what makes the current moment difficult. A line justified by general reliability still lands in a specific backyard, and the homeowner has no particular reason to believe the general justification.

The part that should concern anyone building anything large is that opposition organized around data centers does not stay organized around data centers. Transmission capacity is shared infrastructure. The same 500-kilovolt line that serves a hyperscale campus also serves the industrial park, the hospital expansion, the manufacturing plant, and the thousand-unit residential project that needs an interconnection five years out. Communities that successfully delay or reroute a line are not constraining one development. They are constraining everything downstream of it.

Eminent domain reform is becoming part of the conversation. Property owners who settled with utilities have started arguing publicly that the legal process favors institutions with counsel over individuals without it, and state legislatures are listening in several of the markets where transmission buildout is heaviest. Any procedural changes that result will apply to pipelines, roads, and water infrastructure as readily as to power lines. This might help move projects along in the short term but could result in even more politcal backlash that could

We would expect the political energy currently aimed at data centers to outlast the particular projects that generated it, because the underlying objection is to high-voltage infrastructure crossing residential land rather than to what sits at the end of the wire. Developers in markets with constrained interconnection queues may find that the capacity they are counting on has become harder to build for reasons that have nothing to do with their own project.

item.title: Opportunity Zones Enter Second Phase With Minimal Oversight of Beneficiaries
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Miami's luxury Design District qualifies again for Opportunity Zone tax breaks as the federal program enters its second phase with limited oversight.

The post Opportunity Zones Enter Second Phase With Minimal Oversight of Beneficiaries appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Miami’s Design District, a 30-acre luxury retail corridor where shoppers carry Dior bags past valet lines of Ferraris, qualifies again for federal Opportunity Zone tax breaks when the program’s second phase begins next year. Congress created Opportunity Zones in 2017 to attract investment in lower-income areas by allowing investors to defer or eliminate certain capital-gains taxes. The Design District qualified because census-takers group the retail hub with adjacent lower-income neighborhoods including Little Haiti and Buena Vista. Because the district has no residences, census income calculations rely solely on residential data from the poorer tract perimeters.

Developer Craig Robins, who began transforming the Design District from a depressed area in the 1990s, said he and his partners—L Catterton, backed by LVMH chief Bernard Arnault, and Brookfield—do not pursue the tax breaks directly because they acquired central parcels before 2017. Robins said the designation attracted hundreds of millions of dollars from outside investors to the area, driving land values up and potentially generating hundreds of millions in untaxed profits for owners of qualifying properties. Several major projects underway could qualify for breaks, including a Fouquet’s hotel and a 20-story office tower called Ursa. Census data shows the tract’s residential base remains largely lower-income, raising questions about whether investment reached existing communities.

The program has drawn criticism for lacking public reporting requirements, making tax breaks hard to trace. Brett Theodos of the Urban Institute said Opportunity Zones function as subsidies for high-net-worth investors to make deals they would pursue regardless of incentives. The program’s reliance on census income data up to six years old means designations may not reflect current neighborhood conditions. John Lettieri, whose Economic Innovation Group conceived the program, said governors bear responsibility for selecting appropriate locations despite imperfect data.

item.title: Fitness Is Still the Amenity That Moves Multifamily Leases
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
As multifamily vacancies rise, strategic fitness amenities and wellness programming can help properties attract renters, boost renewals, and stand out.

The post Fitness Is Still the Amenity That Moves Multifamily Leases appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Softening conditions in a growing number of multifamily markets have put owners in a position they have not faced in years. National vacancy has climbed, rent growth has flattened, and roughly 40 percent of advertised units now carry some form of concession. Free rent works as a short-term lever, but it resets every lease cycle and does nothing for the underlying competitiveness of the property.

Amenities are where owners can make a more durable argument, and the decisions around them carry more weight than the line item suggests. Square footage committed to shared space is square footage not generating rent. Programming carries ongoing payroll. Equipment depreciates and requires service. A building that gets those choices right converts common area into a leasing advantage, and one that gets them wrong has built an expensive room nobody uses.

Fitness continues to lead the list of what renters say they want, and Danny Dulkin, President of Development Services for LIVunLtd, connects that durability to how the market reads wellness more broadly. “Fitness and wellness is synonymous with luxury,” he said. “If you look at all of the highly branded communities like Viceroy or Ritz Carlton, wellness is a huge focus.” The association runs in both directions. A property that invests seriously in wellness signals something about its positioning before a prospect has seen a unit.

For some owners that conviction has translated into considerably more space. Industry sizing benchmarks have long put a 300-unit community somewhere between 3,600 and 4,500 square feet of fitness area, and Dulkin says the top of the market has moved well past that. “Three to four thousand square foot facilities were the norm, now we are seeing ten thousand plus,” he said.

Whether that additional space produces a better amenity is a separate question from whether it produces a bigger one. Dulkin has watched enough projects to be skeptical of square footage as the measure. “It is less about a bigger gym and more about how to create an exciting culture in the building,” he said. A large room full of equipment that residents use alone is a different product from a smaller space with classes, instructors, and a reason for people to show up at the same time.

Programming is where that culture gets built, and the staffing assumption that keeps owners from pursuing it is often wrong. Many assume meaningful programming requires a dedicated full-time hire, which is difficult to justify at a single property. “There is a lot of misinformation about programming,” Dulkin said. “Sometimes they need full time management but sometimes they only need part time management and one manager can do multiple buildings.” An operator with several properties in the same market can distribute that cost across the portfolio rather than loading it onto one asset.

The physical design of the space does more work than the equipment selection, which runs counter to how most budgets get allocated. Dulkin puts the comparison in blunt terms. “If you put great equipment in a room with a black floor and white walls, it won’t look the same as no-name equipment in a palace with backlit mirrors and really high-end finishes,” he said. Prospects touring a building are evaluating how a space feels, and finishes, lighting, and mirrors communicate that faster than the brand on a treadmill.

A well-designed facility also gets heavily used, which creates a maintenance obligation that owners frequently underfund. Equipment running daily across hundreds of residents wears out on a schedule, and a gym with two broken machines stops being an amenity. “Try to have at least a little bit of CapEx set aside to improve the facilities, even if it is just keeping everything working well and finding a right service provider,” Dulkin said. “It can really help extend the life of the equipment.” The reserve is modest relative to the original build cost and protects the value of it.

Demographics point toward this continuing rather than cycling out. Fitness centers rank among the amenities younger renters cite most consistently, and the cohort moving into prime renting years has grown up treating physical training as routine rather than optional. We are likely to see the gap widen between properties that treat the gym as a room with equipment in it and those that treat it as a program, with the difference showing up in renewal rates rather than tour counts.

The post Fitness Is Still the Amenity That Moves Multifamily Leases appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Weil Gotshal Collapse Exposes Trophy Office Lease Value Gap
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Weil Gotshal's nearly 450,000-square-foot lease at the GM Building, priced well below market, becomes a contested asset as the firm dissolves.

The post Weil Gotshal Collapse Exposes Trophy Office Lease Value Gap appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Weil, Gotshal & Manges occupies nearly 450,000 square feet across 10 floors of the General Motors Building in Midtown Manhattan, paying roughly $121 per square foot under a lease renewal signed in 2014 that extends through 2034. Brokers estimate current market rates for the firm’s space, which includes some of the building’s best Central Park views, would exceed $200 per square foot. The law firm’s collapse has created uncertainty over whether Weil or the building’s owner, a venture led by BXP, will capture the value of the below-market lease.

If Weil seeks bankruptcy protection, it could attempt to sell the lease to another tenant with court approval, though BXP may challenge whether a replacement tenant can satisfy the lease terms. BXP could instead pay Weil to surrender the lease as the firm dissolves, allowing the landlord to relet the space at current rates. BXP faces a refinancing deadline next year for its 3.43% mortgage on the property, which may give Weil negotiating power and incentivize BXP to resolve the lease question before approaching lenders.

BXP President Doug Linde acknowledged on an earnings call this week that a “vast gap” exists between existing rents at the GM Building and current market rates. Manhattan’s office availability rate dropped to 13.4% in the third quarter, with availability approaching single digits for top-tier space, according to Avison Young. Trophy assets in Midtown have commanded premium rents as major law firms and financial companies compete for prime locations, creating what one broker called a “complete vacuum” of available high-quality space.

item.title: AI Is Letting Everyone in a Real Estate Organization See the Data They Need
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Studio
item.description:
Real estate’s AI adoption is wide but shallow. Everyone drafts and summarizes with it, but almost nobody lets it act. That’s about to change, starting with the stuff that can actually land you in legal trouble.

The post AI Is Letting Everyone in a Real Estate Organization See the Data They Need appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Adoption of AI across real estate organizations has been broad and shallow. Nearly everyone is using it somewhere, usually for drafting, summarizing, or extracting information from documents, and almost nobody has given it authority to decide anything. The human stays in the loop not because the technology cannot handle the task but because handing over judgment feels different from handing over typing.

That boundary is likely to move, though the pace depends less on capability than on comfort. Dai Williams, President of Re-Leased, pointed out that the constraint is often about people rather than models. “The tech is capable of so much but what matters is what humans are comfortable with handing over to AI,” he said. “Once AI shows its effectiveness, it will start to creep in more.” Confidence accumulates through repeated correct outputs, and the organizations further along are the ones that started earlier and have more of that history to draw on.

Live webinar from Re-Leased

Your data is your AI’s ceiling

Thursday, November 19 at 11am PT / 1pm CT

AI can only work with the records behind it. Join Cody Bunea, our VP of Product, for a practical look at how commercial property teams are using AI to capture, check and maintain their data, plus an early look at Credia Monitor, which continuously checks property records and flags what needs attention.

Save your seat

Can’t make it live? Register and we’ll send you the recording.

Underneath the comfort question sits a data question that most portfolios have not resolved. An AI system is working from whatever got entered into the system of record, and real estate data has a long history of being entered inconsistently, incompletely, or incorrectly by people who had other things to do. Williams sees extraction accuracy as the gate that everything else waits behind. “If you can trust the data that gets extracted you can start to automate putting data where it needs to go,” he said. Automating the movement of information is a smaller ask than automating a decision, and it is the step that makes larger ones possible.

The application that has proven itself first is monitoring, which happens to be something AI does well and organizations do poorly. Lease documents contain dozens of dates and conditions that require someone to act before a window closes, and those obligations tend to live in a spreadsheet maintained by whoever inherited it. Rent reviews are the failure Williams encounters most. “The most common things we see missed is rent reviews,” he said. “There is sometimes a lack of ownership on who needs to oversee it.” A missed review locks in below-market rent for the rest of the term, and nobody discovers it until someone reconciles the rent roll against the lease.

Compliance carries a different kind of exposure, which is why Williams thinks it deserves more attention than it usually gets. “Compliance is so important, it is one of the only things that can land you in jail if you don’t do it right,” he said. Fire safety inspections, elevator certifications, environmental testing, and accessibility requirements all run on schedules that vary by jurisdiction and property type, and a portfolio operating across several markets is tracking hundreds of recurring obligations with different triggers.

What exists today mostly flags those lapses. A system notices that a fire extinguisher certification has expired and tells someone. The version coming next closes the loop, ordering the replacement, scheduling the service, and updating the certificate record without a person routing it. Getting there requires an organization willing to let an agent transact on its behalf, which brings the conversation back to where it started.

Query access is changing a different part of the picture, and it is reshaping how platforms get built. Dashboards have always been a compromise between what developers anticipated users wanting and what any individual user actually needs on a given day. Williams describes two populations with incompatible requirements. “There are two types of users, highly specialized and very broad,” he said. “The specialized users are working with tenants will want to be very specific about the data they have. Broad users look at it at a portfolio level and want to see how all of the properties compare with each other.” A property manager needs the detail on one building. An asset manager needs the comparison across forty. Natural language querying serves both without forcing either into a layout designed for the other.

Whether any of this scales depends on something harder than the interface, which is getting an AI system access to information scattered across the platforms different stakeholders use. Property management, accounting, maintenance, and asset management systems each hold part of the picture, and a portfolio view assembled from one of them is incomplete by construction. Williams sees that as the gap between consumer AI and anything usable at an institutional level. “Institutional knowledge is so important, most LLMs are built for single users,” he said. “You need tools that stretch across verticals that can really be used by large organizations.”

The post AI Is Letting Everyone in a Real Estate Organization See the Data They Need appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Semiconductor Manufacturing Fuels Taiwanese Investment Wave Across Arizona Markets
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
TSMC's Arizona expansion pulls $500 million in Taiwanese capital into Phoenix real estate, accelerating home values and industrial demand near the chipmaker's campus.

The post Semiconductor Manufacturing Fuels Taiwanese Investment Wave Across Arizona Markets appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.’s $265 billion Arizona campus has drawn more than $500 million in Taiwanese real estate investment since 2021, matching Canadian capital inflows to the Phoenix region. Family offices and property investors from Taipei are acquiring industrial sites, development parcels, and residential projects within proximity to TSMC’s 2,000-acre north Phoenix facility, which now includes one operational fabrication plant and two more scheduled by decade’s end. Taicoon Property Partners paid $88 million for two plots near the campus, planning a $1 billion mixed-use project anchored by Taiwanese retail brands. Starlux and China Airlines operate nonstop flights between Taipei and Phoenix, and Taiwan opened a trade office in the state capital in 2024.

North Gateway and Desert View submarkets near the TSMC campus recorded 53% home value appreciation over six years, outpacing Phoenix’s 42% citywide gain. Industrial vacancies in northwest Phoenix fell to 8% in June from 16% a year earlier, compared with a two-percentage-point drop across the broader metro area. Howard Hughes accelerated development timelines for Teravalis, a 37,000-acre master-planned community west of Phoenix that will eventually include 110,000 homes and 60 million square feet of retail. Major builders Taylor Morrison and Lennar are expanding across the region, with one submarket planning 3,300 new homes.

TSMC employs 3,500 workers at its Arizona facilities and plans to add 2,500 more, creating demand that outstrips local labor supply for specialized semiconductor roles. The company sponsors visas for Taiwanese workers, a practice that drew a class-action discrimination lawsuit from a former employee alleging favoritism toward East Asian hires. TSMC says many overseas employees are on temporary assignment while it recruits from U.S. universities and local training programs. The administration last month suspended several large tech companies from a permanent residency sponsorship program, and Arizona State University faces a visa fraud investigation tied to foreign graduate enrollment.

Land constraints tied to Arizona groundwater rules and state-owned property sales are surfacing conflicts between residential developers and industrial expansion. TSMC purchased roughly 900 acres within the NorthPark development south of Loop 303, reducing planned housing by 20% despite hundreds of public objections to rezoning. Deer Valley Unified School District now enrolls hundreds of students from Taiwanese families, with the superintendent projecting it will become Arizona’s largest district within two decades. Local brokers report midnight calls from Asian investors asking a single question about any available tract: distance to the TSMC campus.

TSMC’s $265 Billion Campus Is Driving a Real Estate Boom in the Phoenix Suburbs
